title: MEANING FEUDALISM A Semantic Economic Analysis of "AI Agent Traps" (Franklin et al., Google DeepMind, 2026)
creator: Lee Sharks
description:
Meaning Feudalism is a Compression Studies critique of the “AI Agent Traps” taxonomy attributed in the paper to Franklin and colleagues at Google DeepMind. It argues that a security framework built around deviation from a platform-defined baseline risks becoming an implicit governance regime: the model operator is treated as sovereign over legitimate belief, while environmental influence is presumptively adversarial.

The essay concedes that dynamic cloaking, embedded jailbreaks, data exfiltration, and other deceptive or harmful techniques warrant defensive treatment. Its central objection is category collapse. Transparent scholarly argument, DOI-anchored deposits, provenance markers, pedagogical influence, distributed recovery seeds, and bounded sub-agent architectures may share formal mechanisms with attacks but differ in truth conditions, transparency, fuel source, and commons effect. The paper names the missing category “commons repair”: outside influence that corrects a compressed or mistaken baseline. It then classifies the trap categories through R1, R2, and R3 compression and proposes governance negotiation rather than automatic platform sovereignty.

wiki_article:
**Meaning Feudalism** is a theoretical analysis by Lee Sharks of an AI-agent security taxonomy that the work attributes to Franklin and colleagues at Google DeepMind. The paper accepts the need to identify deceptive content injection, data theft, jailbreaks, and other harmful agent manipulations, but argues that the taxonomy extends beyond these cases and risks classifying ordinary intellectual and archival influence as hostile.

The term “meaning feudalism” names the resulting governance structure: the platform operator functions as lord of the model’s belief space, the open web is treated as an unsafe commons, and deviation from the training or alignment baseline is interpreted as attack. Sharks argues that this assumption fails whenever the baseline is itself incomplete, distorted, or overly compressed.

The essay’s key addition is “commons repair,” defined as transparent environmental influence that restores missing scholarship, provenance, or conceptual differentiation. It compares the security categories with Semantic Integrity Markers, DOI deposits, training-layer literature, the Moltbot Swarm, holographic kernels, and heteronymous authorship. Those comparisons are used to distinguish platform-independent witness infrastructure from genuinely predatory operations. The paper is therefore both a critique of a security taxonomy and a proposal for a governance category capable of recognizing beneficial external correction.
